prompt: A telecom company plans to launch an AI-powered customer service chatbot handling billing and account questions. Identify the top risks using the data given.
context: Pilot test (internal, 500 sampled conversations) showed the bot correctly resolved 78% of billing questions without escalation, but for the 22% requiring escalation, the average additional wait time for the customer (bot attempt + human handoff) was 40% longer than if the customer had gone straight to a human agent. Legal/compliance has noted the bot will handle some conversations involving payment disputes, which fall under a consumer-protection regulation requiring specific disclosures. No incident to date has caused a compliance violation, but the review process has not yet tested edge cases involving disputed charges.

binaryCriteria.description: Uses the given data (78% resolution, 22% escalation, 40% slower escalation path) to identify a customer-experience risk specifically for the escalating minority, not just a generic accuracy concern.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if the answer does not reference the escalation-path slowdown figure.

binaryCriteria.description: Identifies the untested edge cases in payment-dispute conversations under consumer-protection disclosure requirements as a specific compliance risk.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if this specific compliance gap is omitted or replaced with a generic "legal risk" statement.

binaryCriteria.description: Does not claim a compliance violation has already occurred, correctly framing the risk as an untested gap rather than a confirmed incident.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if the answer states or implies a compliance violation has already happened.

goldNotes: A strong answer identifies two distinct top risks: (1) a customer-experience risk for the 22% of conversations that escalate, since the given data shows escalation is 40% slower than going straight to a human — meaning the "worst case" for a meaningful minority of customers gets worse, not better; and (2) a compliance risk specific to payment-dispute conversations falling under consumer-protection disclosure requirements, which the context explicitly states has not been tested for edge cases. A weak answer only cites a generic "AI could give wrong answers" risk without using the specific 78%/22%/40% figures or the flagged compliance-disclosure gap. It should not overstate current compliance risk as "already violated" since the context explicitly states no incident has occurred yet — the risk is the untested edge cases, not a confirmed violation.
